analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal cybersecurity office and imposes strict penalties on credit reporting agencies for data breaches.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Elizabeth Warren in December 2024, never received a hearing or vote and died when the Senate Banking Committee took no action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Credit reporting agencies like Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion hold Social Security numbers, account numbers, and other sensitive data on nearly every American adult, but no agency directly supervises their data security. This bill would create a Cybersecurity Office at the FTC to set and enforce strict security standards, require agencies to report breaches within 10 days and notify affected consumers, and automatically fine them $100 per consumer whose name and data were exposed, with penalties capped at 50% of the agency's gross revenue (up to 75% if they fail to report on time). Half of every penalty would go to the breach victims themselves.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans whose most sensitive personal data sits in credit bureau databases. They would get faster breach notification, publicly posted breach notices, automatic compensation when a breach exposed their information, and lower odds of an Equifax-scale leak in the first place because the FTC could force security fixes and sue violators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose data credit bureaus hold

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Office of Cybersecurity at the FTC that supervises covered consumer reporting agencies and writes mandatory data security rules, including encryption, patching, network monitoring, and data minimization [S2].

Requires a covered agency to notify the FTC within 10 days of a breach and to notify affected consumers and post a public notice on an expeditious timeline, with limited delays only for law enforcement or national security reasons [S2].

Mandates a civil penalty of $100 for each consumer whose name plus one other identifying item was exposed, plus $50 per additional item exposed, with the cap at 50% of the agency's prior-year gross revenue — doubled to 75% if the agency missed the reporting deadline or violated the security standards [S2].
Directs that half of every penalty be divided among the consumers affected by the breach, and leaves consumers free to sue under state or other federal law on top of the federal penalty [S2].
Authorizes $100 million to fund the office's inspections, research, and enforcement [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The credit reporting industry bears the compliance costs and the automatic penalties, and would pass some of those costs to lenders and businesses that buy credit reports. The $100 million for the new office would come from federal appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit reporting agencies and their business customers

drawbacks.text: The penalty formula is strict liability: a breach exposing even one person's information triggers a $100-per-consumer action, and the fee schedule applies per item of data, so a large breach at a major bureau could produce penalties near the 50%-of-revenue cap regardless of how good the agency's security actually was [S2].

Compliance with the required technical measures — continuous monitoring, encryption, penetration testing, documentation — is costly, and agencies would likely pass some of those costs on to the businesses that buy credit reports and, indirectly, to consumers [S2].
The bill covers consumer reporting agencies only, so the many other companies holding the same kinds of sensitive data would remain outside this regime [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real gap: credit bureaus hold the crown jewels of identity theft data with no dedicated security regulator, and the Equifax breach of 2017 exposed roughly half the country. The compensation and notification rights are concrete consumer wins. The strict, revenue-based penalties are the main design risk — they could punish agencies harshly even for diligent security — though the trade-off is deliberate: it gives the bureaus a powerful financial reason to invest in protection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Data Breach Prevention and Compensation Act of 2024 in the Senate on December 5, 2024, with Senators Mark Warner and Jeanne Shaheen as cosponsors [S1][S2][S3].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, the committee with jurisdiction over credit reporting law [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and no floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting agencies are better off: they never faced the automatic penalties and mandatory security standards, and consumers remain without federal breach compensation from the bureaus.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on December 5, 2024.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral (Democratic-chaired in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on December 5, 2024 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill died in a Democratic-chaired committee without ever reaching a recorded vote, so the parties' positions were never tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion and other large bureaus)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed mandatory security standards, annual examinations, 10-day breach reporting, and automatic penalties of $100 per affected consumer capped at 50–75% of gross revenue — a direct cost to an industry that profits from selling consumers' personal data. Its interest ran against the bill's consumer protections, which is precisely why stricter oversight of these bureaus never advanced.

industries.industry: Businesses that buy credit reports (lenders, landlords, insurers)
industries.note: They would face slightly higher report costs as bureaus passed on compliance and penalty expenses, but would also benefit from a more secure data ecosystem and fewer large-scale fraud waves after breaches.
